rows: I can teach them everything I know. I can't teach them to want it.
Brawling? I have done plenty of it. The sensible version is the one that keeps you working.
A bet is paid for with someone else's knees. Think about that before you take it.
Patience is a good habit to keep. Patience is the first thing I try to teach.
The people deserve work done properly. That is what I want to show them, even at my age.
I am here, I am still good, and I am still honest.
I am not finished, whatever some of you think. I am still doing the job.
Look at the stance and remember it. It is the one I taught the young ones. Copy it.
You bring up technique. Good. Show me one hold you could teach to a beginner tomorrow.
Strikes are for the right moment. The right moment is not every second.
A gamble you cannot afford is one you should not take. Think about who pays for it.
A stall is a bad habit. I have spent years trying to break young people of it.
The people want a contest they can respect. Give them one, and I will do the same.
You say I am finished. I say I am still able to teach. Watch me do it.
You are proud of your {strength}. Good, but it must be taught. Sensible. Now show me the discipline behind it.
I have watched your {strength}, and I can see where the young ones go wrong with it.
You did not flinch. That matters. Sensible. Calm is the first thing a young one learns from me.
Good point, that. You have listened, and that is half the battle.
I could be sharp about that. I'll be patient. I would rather be honest and let you think about it.
One pin. Learn it. Keep me down, and I will tell you exactly what you did well.
On the mat we go slowly. I want you to feel every step.
Grounded or standing, the lesson is the same. Look after yourself and the other person.
Stay in front of me, and show me you understand the lesson.
A better answer. Keep learning. That is what I was hoping to hear.
You have sidestepped it. Take your time and answer plainly.
Good point, that. That is a lesson worth remembering.
I will let that teaching stand. We test it at the bell, lesson by lesson.
I will wrestle this match carefully, and I will show the young ones how it is done.
My approach is steady, the way I teach. You will see the lesson on the night.
Whatever happens, I want the young ones watching to learn something.
The lesson is still open. There is still a lesson to give.
I have one challenge left, and you will hear it plainly when the bell rings.
You're right to ask, lad or not. A teacher must be able to demonstrate the point, and I cannot demonstrate that one.
I won't teach anyone to make accusations without backing them up. I should take my own advice.
Good. Knowing when to take a word back is worth learning. Now we wrestle.
Fair enough. Let the lesson be in the ring, not in a claim you cannot establish.
Watch whether we can still wrestle properly when we're tired. That's a test I'd give any of the young ones.
The result and the way we earn it are there for everyone to see. Do the job properly and let them judge.
Leave the accusation aside. What can we demonstrate in the ring that these young ones could learn from?
What can we show the people by wrestling properly, rather than asking them to take our word for it?
